The NUF solution reduces to the uniform-flux (UF) solution when the number of flux segments is set to one. Parametric analysis reveals that partial circumferential screen blockage mainly produces a localized near-well effect under constant-rate test (CRT) conditions, whereas its influence can persist throughout almost the entire flow domain under constant-head test (CHT) conditions. Across all conditions, NUF predictions fall between the UF and fully penetrating-well solutions and are consistently closer to the latter, indicating that the UF assumption overestimates the mitigating effect of the non-screened region. These findings establish the NUF model as a more accurate framework for interpreting pumping or injection tests in wells affected by circumferential clogging and improve understanding of flow behaviour in circumferentially partially clogged wells.

title: Hydrologic and economic performance of groundwater-conservation policies for agricultural and residential water use in the Oklahoma Ogallala Aquifer
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Jeffrey D. Vitale, Frank A. Ward
abstract: Groundwater depletion threatens irrigated agriculture and rural household water security across the High Plains, yet the hydrologic and economic consequences of alternative pumping institutions remain poorly resolved at county scale. This study develops a spatially disaggregated hydroeconomic optimization model for agricultural and residential groundwater use in seven Oklahoma counties overlying the Ogallala Aquifer during 2016–2021. The framework integrates county-specific aquifer geometry, measured water-level trends, pumping depths, crop acreage, evapotranspiration, crop prices, household demand, and groundwater pumping costs. Positive mathematical programming calibrates agricultural land and water use to observed conditions, while a calibrated inverse-demand system represents residential use. Five institutional regimes are compared: unrestricted pumping, cap-and-trade, proportional cap-and-share, urban-priority allocation, and irrigation-priority allocation. The four conservation scenarios impose the same terminal water-table target and the same stress-test assumption of one-half of the calibrated recharge flux; therefore, comparisons among the four conservation rules isolate allocation effects, whereas differences from the unrestricted baseline reflect both the tighter terminal target and the lower recharge assumption. Under cap-and-trade, cumulative irrigation pumping falls from about 3.48 to 2.14 million acre-feet, while most residential use is preserved. Cap-and-share achieves a similar terminal outcome but imposes larger economic costs in several counties. Urban priority nearly preserves historical residential use, whereas irrigation priority transfers most shortages to households. County outcomes vary because of differences in saturated thickness, pumping depth, irrigated acreage, crop mix, and measured decline. The findings show that, under a common conservation stress test, institutional rules strongly affect where pumping reductions occur and who bears their economic cost.

title: Response-pattern-aware graph neural network for rapid compound rainfall-tide urban drainage prediction
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Peiyuan Sun, Maochuan Hu, Kui Xu, Yongjie Wong, Bingjun Liu, Xiaohong Chen
abstract: Rapid compound rainfall-tide drainage prediction supports multi-scenario assessment in coastal cities, but network-wide surrogate errors can obscure high-response nodes, dynamic hotspots and peak-recession behavior. This study develops RPAG-GNN, a SWMM-supervised graph surrogate for rapid same-network node-level hydraulic-head prediction and response-oriented diagnostic analysis. RPAG-GNN combines drainage topology, historical hydraulic states, antecedent tide-memory descriptors and prescribed rainfall-tide forcing within a response-supervised residual-update allocation framework. During training, SWMM-derived response-state, peak-intensity and phase-evolution cues guide a bounded gate that allocates node- and step-specific residual head updates. In the fixed Cuiping catchment, 832 candidate scenarios were constructed from 64 rainfall and 13 tide-boundary processes, and 160 mutually exclusive events were used for training, validation, independent testing and pressure testing. Node responses were strongly heterogeneous: median response amplitude was 0.91 m, the 95th percentile reached 4.37 m and four response regimes were identified. RPAG-GNN achieved node-event median main and high-response RMSE values of 0.151 and 0.266 m; the corresponding event-level medians were 0.328 and 0.450 m, and pressure-test medians were 0.462 and 0.614 m. Median peak-timing error was 5 min, gate activation correlated strongly with response amplitude (Spearman ρ = 0.829), tide-memory gain concentrated in medium- and high-tide-imprint nodes, and a representative event showed 89.39–98.48% hotspot overlap. These results support response-supervised update allocation for same-network compound drainage prediction within the tested Cuiping topology, without implying direct inundation mapping, operational warning issuance or cross-network validation.

title: Monthly dynamics of global surface water from 2015 to 2023
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Xiaoyang Guo, Yuchen Liu, R.Iestyn Woolway, Ting Du, Lai Lai, Yongqi Sun, Yanjun Tian, Yongnian Gao
abstract: Surface water plays a central role in regulating global water, energy, and biogeochemical cycles, yet its strong spatial and temporal variability makes consistent monitoring difficult. Existing global products have greatly advanced surface water mapping, but they still struggle to combine fine spatial detail, monthly continuity, and reliable observations under frequent cloud cover. Here, we developed the High precision Global Monthly Surface Water dataset (HGMSW), a 10 m monthly surface water record from 2015 to 2023. The framework combines Sentinel 1 SAR and Sentinel 2 multispectral observations in a complementary way. Sentinel 2 time series imagery was used to construct a noise reduced maximum inundation extent, while monthly Sentinel 1 VV backscatter composites were used with the Calibrated Edge Otsu configuration to delineate water dynamics within this spatial constraint. Global validation showed that HGMSW achieved an overall accuracy of 97.59%, an F1 score of 97.55%, and a Kappa coefficient of 95.18%. The correct classification rate for small water bodies reached 88.83%, demonstrating the advantage of 10 m mapping for fragmented water features. Independent monthly validation using 3 m PlanetScope imagery across nine representative regions yielded a mean overall accuracy of 97.8%, confirming the ability of HGMSW to capture monthly boundary dynamics. HGMSW revealed a global monthly mean surface water area of 2.95 × 106 km2 during 2017–2021, with an average annual growth rate of 2.08%. The dataset further identified stronger seasonal variability in Northern Hemisphere continents, weaker variability in ocean influenced Southern Hemisphere regions, a weak bimodal pattern in Africa, and basin scale disruptions associated with droughts, floods, and reservoir impoundment. HGMSW fills an important gap between long term 30 m water products and static 10 m land cover datasets, providing a spatially detailed monthly record for monitoring surface water dynamics and their responses to climate variability and human regulation.

title: Shifting controls on DIC export in the Doce River Basin during baseflow conditions: from rock weathering to anthropogenic forcing
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Isadora Mello, Eduardo Duarte Marques, Daniela Vasconcelos Machado, Rafael Tarantino Amarante, Eduardo Paim Víglio, Emmanoel Vieira Silva-Filho
abstract: Tropical rivers play a disproportionately important role in global carbon fluxes, yet they remain underrepresented in biogeochemical datasets. This study investigated the fluvial fluxes of Dissolved Inorganic Carbon (DIC) and dominant hydrochemical processes in 499 small tropical rivers and streams across the Doce River Basin (DRB), Brazil, a region affected by the 2015 Fundão Dam collapse, the world’s largest mining tailings dam failure and Brazil’s most severe environmental disaster. Water samples were collected during dry-season baseflow conditions in 2010. Surface-water chemistry reflects the combined influence of silicate weathering and anthropogenic inputs, with a mean DIC fluvial flux of 5.44 kg C km−2 day−1. Rock weathering is the dominant basin-scale control on DIC concentrations, as indicated by a factor explaining 40.6% of the total hydrochemical variance (Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+, HCO3 −), consistent with the basin’s predominantly silicate lithology and localized contributions from carbonate-bearing units upstream. Anthropogenic inputs act as a secondary but systematic control, particularly in the midstream sector, where pasture land use is associated with higher DIC concentrations (r = +0.448, p < 0.001), while mining and urban effluents locally enrich alkalinity and major ions. Micro-basins dominated by natural land cover show lower mean DIC concentrations (5.24 mg C L−1) than anthropogenically influenced sub-basins (11.13 mg C L−1), a 2.1-fold difference. As these results derive from a single dry-season campaign, they should not be extrapolated to an annual DIC budget. Overall, this study provides a hydrogeochemical characterization of tributary systems in the DRB, supporting future monitoring and environmental assessment efforts.

title: Learning water diversion behaviour in regulated river networks using graph neural networks and neural decision trees
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Moritz Wirthensohn, Ye Tuo, Markus Disse
abstract: Human water diversions alter river dynamics and are difficult to represent when operational rules are uncertain or discontinuous. This study investigates how graph-based deep learning models represent diversion behaviour in river networks under varying degrees of prior operational knowledge. Using SWAT+ simulations as an internally consistent synthetic benchmark, we design controlled diversion scenarios of increasing rule complexity. We compare graph attention networks that embed river network topology and diversion connectivity directly into their model structure, with no prior operational information, with partial structural constraints, with fully prescribed rules applied in post-processing, and with a hybrid architecture that explicitly separates hydrological prediction from operational decision-making via a Neural Decision Tree. All approaches reproduce total flow before diversion robustly, while diverted flow skill declines with operational complexity. Additional operational knowledge does not consistently improve predictive accuracy, as diversion errors are dominated by propagation from total-flow uncertainty. The hybrid model achieves comparable skill while providing explicit and analysable decision representations, highlighting trade-offs between flexibility, robustness, and interpretability. The modular and structurally explicit formulation illustrates how graph-based AI components can support transparent and interpretable representations of operational decision-making in regulated river systems, though validation across diverse catchments and real-world operational conditions remains necessary.

title: Climate change both increases and decreases winter snowmelt across North America
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Shadi Hatami, Masoud Zaerpour, André S. Ballarin, Rahim Barzegar, Simon Michael Papalexiou, Alain Pietroniro, Jan Franklin Adamowski
abstract: Snowmelt, a vital source of freshwater for a large portion of North America’s population, is increasingly vulnerable to the impact of climate change. Air temperature and precipitation are significant climatic controllers regulating snowmelt dynamics. In this study, we quantified the response of winter snowmelt magnitude to changing temperature and precipitation across North America (Canada and the United States) using gridded, observation-driven data and future projections. Our analysis of far-future conditions (2091-2100) reveals a significant increase (>60%) in winter (November-March) snowmelt in northern latitudes, while southern latitudes are projected to experience a decline (<38%). Projected snowmelt changes are strongly associated with changes in winter temperature, while projected declines are consistent with regions experiencing reduced snowfall under warming climates. Our findings suggest that the probability of an increase in winter snowmelt is high under the warmer and wetter climatic conditions prevailing in northern regions. In contrast, winter snowmelt across southern latitudes is likely to decrease. Plain language summary Snowmelt plays a critical role in sustaining water resources for large populations across North America. As temperature and precipitation are major climatic factors regulating snowmelt dynamics, changes in these variables can affect the magnitude of snowmelt. Given projected climate change, it is essential to assess the vulnerability of snowmelt magnitude to changing temperatures and precipitation to understand future water availability. Our analysis of future winter snowmelt under compound changes in air temperature and precipitation across North America indicates that winter snowmelt could increase by 60% in many regions of Canada. In contrast, in southern areas, the winter snowmelt volume could decrease by as much as 38%. These results suggest that warmer winters are the primary driver of increased snowmelt, while reduced snowfall primarily governs the projected snowmelt declines.

title: Benchmarking a bounded-coordinate DeepONet for unsaturated flow and solute transport under time-varying infiltration
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Zhitong Ma, Xueyang Sun, Wenke Wang, Jing Li, Shuyao Ma
abstract: Repeated solution of the Richards and advection–dispersion equations can make large-scale ensemble evaluation of unsaturated-flow and solute-transport scenarios computationally restrictive. We evaluate RegShift-DeepONet, a bounded-coordinate variant of Shift-DeepONet that receives a time-varying infiltration hydrograph q top ( t ) and soil hydraulic parameters and predicts pressure head h ( z , t ) and concentration c ( z , t ) . The tanh -bounded affine transform is treated as a guardrail on coordinate adaptation rather than as a hard physical constraint. Five architectures are compared using common data splits, three random seeds, and parity in training budgets under in-distribution (IID), high-peak, and late-peak forcing tests. For the median sample-wise concentration relative L 2 error, the bounded model obtains 0.0617 ± 0.0023 , 0.0714 ± 0.0081 , and 0.0692 ± 0.0096 , respectively. The corresponding unconstrained Shift-DeepONet errors are 0.0612 ± 0.0115 , 0.0698 ± 0.0136 , and 0.0753 ± 0.0158 . Thus, their differences under IID and high-peak forcing are smaller than the observed three-seed variability, while bounding reduces concentration error by 8.1% under the late-peak shift. A tuned Fourier neural operator gives errors of 0.1184 − − 0.1305 . Supplementary temporal-shape and joint forcing–soil stress tests delineate the conditions under which process-model confirmation is required. Mass-balance error is used as a conservative trigger for HYDRUS review rather than as a stand-alone accuracy certificate. The results support a focused conclusion: bounded coordinate adaptation can selectively stabilise temporal extrapolation, with applicability checks and HYDRUS confirmation providing an auditable screening workflow.

title: Understanding data sufficiency and temporal informativeness for hydrological model calibration in data scarce regions
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Velpuri Manikanta, Surya Kiran Guniganti, Daneti Arun Sourya, Rathinasamy Maheswaran
abstract: Reliable hydrological model calibration is often constrained by limited continuous discharge records, yet it remains unclear whether the amount and timing of calibration data required by a catchment can be predicted in advance from its physical characteristics. This study develops and tests an a priori predictive framework using Classification and Regression Tree (CART) analysis and Symbolic Regression to estimate calibration data requirements and identify the most informative calibration period. The framework was evaluated across 671 catchments in the United States, including 477 rainfall-dominated and 194 snow-dominated catchments, using calibration periods spanning one month to one year. CART identified mean annual precipitation, snow fraction, aridity, and soil depth as dominant controls on performance loss under sparse calibration. Symbolic Regression, incorporating dynamic meteorological inputs and static catchment attributes, derived compact analytical expressions for predicting the optimal calibration month. Results show that calibration requirements depend more on hydrologic regime and seasonal process dynamics than on calibration length alone. One-month calibration reproduced benchmark performance in 23% (110/477) of rainfall-dominated catchments, whereas 44% (85/194) of snow-dominated catchments required 12 months to represent snowmelt and storage dynamics adequately. Higher aridity and evapotranspiration variability increased sensitivity to sparse calibration. Objective function choice also affected calibration performance because different metrics emphasize different hydrograph segments. Together, these results provide a process-oriented, data-driven framework for identifying when limited discharge records can support reliable calibration and anticipating these requirements a priori in new or ungauged catchments.

title: Hydroclimatic seasonality, bacterioplankton, and dissolved organic matter in a semi-enclosed plateau lake
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Wei Zheng, Fan Xia, Qian Bao, Yalan Zhu, Muzi Li, Xiaoyan Tang
abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is a central component of carbon cycling, yet the associations among hydroclimatic conditions, bacterioplankton communities, and DOM composition remain insufficiently understood in plateau lakes. This study investigated the seasonal variation of chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM) and its associations with bacterioplankton communities in Qionghai Lake, a semi-enclosed plateau lake in southwestern China. Across the four sampling campaigns, CDOM exhibited a strong autochthonous and microbial signature, with protein-like components accounting for 53.2% of the total fluorescence. CDOM abundance peaked in autumn, when aCDOM(355) reached 1.94 ± 0.24 m−1, coinciding with elevated concentrations of TN and NH4 +-N and a higher contribution from the microbial humic-like component C1. In contrast, winter exhibited the lowest aCDOM(355) (0.85 ± 0.23 m−1), the highest Ca2+ concentrations, and the lowest contribution from the tryptophan-like component C4. Bacterioplankton communities also showed clear seasonal shifts, and network analysis identified different bacterial assemblages associated with humic-like and protein-like CDOM fractions. At the annual scale, partial least squares path modeling revealed contrasting microbial patterns: nutrient conditions were positively related to α-diversity, which was inversely related to microbial CDOM, whereas physicochemical conditions were more strongly related to β-diversity, which covaried positively with terrestrial CDOM. Overall, seasonal hydroclimatic variation was accompanied by shifts in CDOM abundance, composition, and bacterioplankton community structure, providing new insights into seasonal carbon cycling and bacterioplankton–DOM linkages in plateau lakes.

title: Real-time control of rainwater harvesting in an urban catchment: a model predictive control approach under forecasting uncertainty
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Ofer Snir, Eran Friedler, Luca Vezzaro
abstract: Rainwater harvesting (RWH) is gaining popularity in urban water systems as a tool to address the challenges posed by urbanization and climate change. Urban areas face water scarcity and increased runoff due to growing population and the conversion of natural areas into impermeable surfaces. RWH systems can serve as stormwater control measures while storing and supplying rainwater for non-potable uses. However, RWH systems become less effective as storm events exceed their storage capacity. To overcome this limitation, the field of real-time controlled RWH systems has emerged in the latest research. These systems release water from tanks before and during significant rain events, reducing uncontrolled overflows. This study examines the effects of favourable control policies on an urban catchment retrofitted with RWH systems. A simulation-optimisation procedure is developed to generate flexible control policies that adapt to changing rainfall forecasts using concepts from the Model Predictive Control approach. The methodology aims to reduce peak flows, minimise rainwater release, and optimise a single objective function without complex procedures. The methodology is evaluated through simulations of 73 rain events in a case study catchment. The MPC achieved a median peak flow reduction of 29% while maintaining low rainwater availability losses (median rainwater availability reduction: 1.5–2.0%). Forecast uncertainty had only a minor impact on performance, and the MPC consistently outperformed rule-based control strategies, providing superior flood mitigation while preserving stored rainwater. The results show promising outcomes in mitigating flows while maximising water availability, suggesting potential to enhance urban resilience.

title: Coastal aquifer modification of dissolved barium during submarine groundwater discharge to a semi-enclosed bay
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Yancheng Wang, Guangquan Chen, Shan Sun, Shibin Zhao, Jianing Zhang, Xiaowei Wang, Guiyao Xiong, Lijun Song, Xinbin Zhao, Liyuan Pan, Xingyong Xu
abstract: Submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) is increasingly recognized as a crucial vector for transporting trace elements to the ocean, yet the mobilization and liberation process of dissolved barium (Ba) at the land–ocean interface of semi-enclosed bays remains poorly constrained. In this study, a multi-isotope tracer (224Ra, 226Ra and 222Rn) approach was employed to elucidate the multi-scale SGD processes in Laizhou Bay, China, a typical semi-enclosed bay. Input parameters were assigned probability distributions based on the observed data using Monto Carlo simulations, and further incorporated into the Ra and Rn mass balance model for calculation. Thus, the result provides a wide range of estimates of the uncertainty associated with SGD flux. The median SGD was 5.38 × 108 m3 d-1 (14.87 cm d-1) in Laizhou Bay, specifically median terrestrial groundwater discharge (TGD) was 0.96 × 108 m3 d-1 (2.66 cm d-1) and median recirculating seawater discharge (RSGD) was 3.24 × 108 m3 d-1 (8.94 cm d-1). SGD-derived Ba fluxes are shown to play a major role in regulating the oceanic Ba budget. The estimated net SGD-derived Ba fluxes ranged from 0.58 × 1010 mg d-1 to 3.19 × 1010 mg d-1, accounting for approximately 32 to 72% of the total terrigenous input. RSGD plays a dominant role in the SGD process, the net Ba flux carried by RSGD is about twice that of TGD. Dissolved Ba exhibited pronounced non-conservative behavior within the coastal aquifer. Sediment-water interactions during seawater-groundwater mixing enhanced dissolved Ba mobilization, increasing the Ba carried by groundwater discharge to Laizhou Bay. Furthermore, due to the long-term neglect of the migration behavior of Ba in groundwater, the Ba flux driven by TGD has been underestimated by approximately 61%. These findings challenge the traditional methods for estimating the SGD-derived solute flux and emphasize that different forms and mobilization of solute in the coastal aquifer should be taken into account.

title: Tracing the journey of size-fractionated particles in the river-to-estuary continuum: insights from short-lived 210 Bi
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Jie Tian, Weifeng Yang, Min Chen, Ziming Fang, Minfang Zheng, Mengya Chen
abstract: Riverine particles deliver an enormous amount of material to the sea; however, their transport along the river-to-coast continuum remains poorly constrained due to a lack of tools capable of resolving large changes over short timescales. Here, we present the first examination of short-lived 210Bi (T 1/2 = 5.01 d) in size-fractionated particles (>60 μm, 10–60 μm, 3–10 μm), together with 210Pb and particulate components, along a river-to-estuary transect. In river water, both δ13C and C/N evidenced the predominantly autochthonous origin of POC, though lithogenics accounted for 77 ± 16% of particles. In contrast to the 210Bi deficit in 10–60 μm fraction, the 210Bi/210Pb equilibrium for > 60 μm indicated a dominant terrestrial origin for > 60 μm particles and minimal conversion between the two sizes. The correlation between POC and 210Bi supports the use of 210Bi to trace the cycling of POC. The greater 210Bi deficit for 10–60 μm and the higher specific activities of 210Bi and 210Pb for 3–10 μm support an overall disaggregation and/or reorganization of 10–60 μm organo-mineral complexes into 3–10 μm fraction. In estuarine surface water, both the greater 210Bi deficit for 3–10 μm and the comparable specific activities of 210Bi or 210Pb to those in the 10–60 μm fraction indicate an aggregation of 3–10 μm POC. The 210Bi-derived transport rates highlight the settling of most particles within the mid-salinity zone (∼10–22), and <33% of riverine POC reached the open sea. This study reveals that available riverine carbon export to the ocean is largely overestimated.

title: Heavy metal accumulation and biological responses at sediment-microplastic interface in hyporheic zone: the importance of dissolved organic matter
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Bingjie Li, Jiayuan Feng, Jinxi Song, Qi Li, Ruichen Mao, Wanying Xu
abstract: The competitive adsorption of heavy metals (HMs) in the river hyporheic zone at the interface between sediments and microplastics (MPs) poses a serious threat to aquatic organisms and ecological safety. Focusing on HMs pollution in the Beiluo River hyporheic zone, a typical river on the Loess Plateau, this study systematically explored the multi-interface distribution characteristics of HMs, the potential mediating role of dissolved organic matter (DOM), and its impact on periphytic algae. Per unit mass, MPs exhibited a strong accumulation potential for HMs (As, Pb, Cr, Cu, and Cd). DOM in the hyporheic zone was mainly composed of micro-sourced humic-like, endogenous protein-like, and terrestrial humic-like; its spatial evolution was driven by redox conditions, salinity background, and adsorption of mineral cations. Statistical modeling suggests that DOM is closely associated with the interface distribution of HMs, directly driving and indirectly transferring them from the external environment. High-molecular-weight terrestrial humic-like substances promote the accumulation of HMs in sediments, whereas low-molecular-weight protein-like and microplastic-heavy metal (MP-HM) have a more closely related distribution pattern. Most importantly, HMs pollution in sediments has a high explanatory power on the biomass of periphytic algae, and the interaction between MP-HM and DOM significantly drives the distribution of periphytic algae. This finding deepens the understanding of the driving mechanism of composite pollution in complex systems and provides scientific support for the bioremediation and refined ecological management of emerging pollutants in watersheds.

title: Ensembling or not? On the value of boosting and bagging for physics-aware machine learning in hydrology
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Adoubi Vincent De Paul Adombi
abstract: Ensemble machine learning methods such as bagging and boosting are widely used to improve predictive performance in hydrological modeling. However, their value when applied to physics-aware machine learning (PaML) models remains largely unexplored. This study investigates whether ensemble strategies provide tangible predictive gains over a standalone PaML model for streamflow simulation. Four controlled experiments were conducted on five representative catchments from the Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies dataset for the contiguous United States (CAMELS-US) to evaluate the influence of training epochs, base learner capacity, ensemble size, and training data length. Bagging, classical boosting, and a growth-based boosting formulation inspired by GrowNet were compared against both weak and well-configured single PaML models. Predictive performance was assessed using the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) and the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE). Results show that ensemble strategies do not yield substantial improvements over a properly configured standalone PaML model, despite requiring greater computational resources. While classical boosting can compensate for intentionally reduced model capacity by aggregating low-capacity PaML learners, the resulting gains remain marginal relative to a moderately expressive single model. Bagging provides limited additional benefits, and the growth-based boosting formulation exhibits non-monotonic and basin-dependent behavior. Overall, the findings suggest that, within the investigated framework, refining the architecture and capacity of a single PaML model is generally more effective than adopting ensemble strategies. These results contribute to clarifying the practical role of ensemble learning in physics-aware hydrological modeling.

title: A historical data curation (HDC) framework integrated with GIS-based multi-criteria decision analysis to inform flood risk prioritization in data-scarce regions
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Rouya Hdeib, Chadi Abdallah, François Colin, Hassan Sabeh, Roger Moussa
abstract: Data-scarce regions lack reliable long-term gauging records and standardized flood databases which constrains classical flood risk assessments and fail to adequately reflect local contexts. Global initiatives emphasize investments in non-traditional data curation to improve the representation of vulnerability and to transform how disaster risk is addressed, complementing systematic flood risk assessment strategies. In this study, we present the outcomes of past flood information curation from newspapers and archives to build a national flood database and evaluate the basin-scale flood risk. We particularly propose a reproducible Historical Data Curation– Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (HDC–MCDA) framework that transforms qualitative historical archives into standardized quantitative Curated Historical Flood Descriptors (CFD) and integrates them with conventional GIS-based MCDA flood risk analysis. We curated a database of 700 flood events (1955–2020) in Lebanon with documented description and impacts. Two CFD, Historical Flood Occurrence (Ne) and Historical Flood Severity (Sev), were developed through text processing and integrated in the MCDA analysis. The study was applied for 16 basins, where hazard and vulnerability are represented by conventional morphological, hydrological and land-use descriptors extracted from available data. Across the studied scenarios, HDC-MCDA led to notable shift in flood risk level, suggesting that HDC captures the realized impact and recalibrates flood risk prioritization by perceived impact information that is often not reflected by scarce hazard and vulnerability data. The study provides a reproducible framework for “soft” documentary data curation and integration into risk assessments, informing prioritization of mitigation and early warning efforts in data-scarce countries.

title: A dual-threshold framework for antecedent wetness controls on hydrological connectivity and nitrate source dynamics in a subtropical agricultural watershed
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Jia Zhou, Hao Wu, Yucang Wang, Xinyi Jiao, Yuhan Han, Hongrui Wu, Qi Ling, Yi Pan, Zheqi Pan, Sijie Li, Kexin Xu, Guangle Dong, Xiaochen Liu, Minpeng Hu, Dingjiang Chen
abstract: Season-based hydrological classifications often fail to resolve the short-term wetness controls that reorganize connectivity and nitrate transport in monsoon-influenced agricultural catchments. To address this issue, daily precipitation and discharge records (1980–2023) were combined with monthly hydrochemical monitoring and dual isotopes of water (δ2H-H2O, δ18O-H2O) and nitrate (δ15N-NO3 –, δ18O-NO3 –; 2014–2023) from six monitoring sites in a subtropical agricultural watershed in eastern China. A 7-day antecedent precipitation index (API7) and the daily baseflow index (BFI) identified two operational thresholds: 34.3 mm for initial hydrological activation and 133 mm for saturated connectivity. These thresholds partitioned the hydrologic record into Baseflow, Transition, and Storm regimes, representing 68.4 %, 29.2 %, and 2.4 % of the record, respectively. Water isotopes showed that the first threshold mainly reflected increased discharge through displacement of stored, evaporatively enriched pre-event water, whereas the second threshold marked a stronger contribution of event water and a pronounced decline in specific conductance. In contrast, riverine NO3 – concentrations changed only modestly at most sites. However, NO3 – isotopes and MixSIAR revealed marked regime-dependent source reorganization in spite of the weak concentration response, with lower δ15N-NO3 – values and shifts in the relative contributions of fertilizer-, soil-, and sewage-derived NO3 – across human-impacted sub-catchments. Random Forest analyses further showed that specific conductance and δ15N-NO3 – remained consistent predictors of NO3 – variability, whereas antecedent wetness, dissolved oxygen, and δ18O-H2O became more influential under Storm conditions. Overall, antecedent wetness governed not only runoff partitioning but also when cryptic NO3 – source switching became hydrologically expressed, providing a process-based alternative to conventional dry/wet seasonal classification.

title: Multivariate and hydrochemical assessment of rivers and groundwater in the Mediterranean Besòs basin (Spain)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Luciana Scrinzi, Anna Jurado, Sandra Pérez, Estanislao Pujades-Garnes
abstract: In the context of climate change, integrated strategies to preserve water quantity and quality in Mediterranean basins are increasingly needed. Here, we investigate hydrochemical patterns of rivers and aquifers in the Besòs basin (NE Spain) and assess how hydrological variability influences these patterns at basin scale. Long-term monitoring data (2007–2024) from river stations and wells were analysed using site-level median concentrations of major ions and nutrients, wet-dry contrasts, flow and groundwater level time series, and multivariate statistical analyses. Groundwater shows higher Ca2+, HCO3 - and NO3 - concentrations, particularly in forested and agricultural areas, consistent with recharge and carbonate mineralization. Lower concentrations in wells close to rivers are consistent with groundwater-river interactions, including groundwater discharge and local mixing along losing reaches. River waters display higher pH and lower geogenic solute concentrations, consistent with groundwater influence and dilution by runoff. Spatial salinity patterns in both compartments are associated with Na+, Cl- and K+ inputs from urban and industrial land use and with dilution capacity. In impacted sites, Na+ and Cl- may dominate over Ca2+ and HCO3 - and are often accompanied by higher TOC and PO4 3-. Rivers’ salinity-related ions increase during low-flow periods, sometimes exceeding groundwater concentrations, whereas concentrations decrease during high-flow periods indicating rainfall-driven dilution. Groundwater-related ions show limited sensitivity to hydrological variability, consistent with a buffered origin. Overall, groundwater-river connectivity and land use are associated with spatial hydrochemical patterns, while hydrological variability modulates dilution and anthropogenic influence.

title: A path-driven structural evolution framework for SWRC hysteresis inspired by pore expansion and contraction processes
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Shiwei Zheng, Gang Chen, Chuanhai Wang, Yue Yu
abstract: Despite extensive development of soil water retention curve (SWRC) models, hysteresis effects are often neglected or represented in simplified forms, and a generally applicable approach for incorporating hysteresis into conventional formulations remains limited. This study presents a path-driven structural evolution framework for modeling SWRC hysteresis, inspired by pore expansion and contraction processes. The proposed framework introduces a hysteresis mechanism into conventional SWRC models through four additional parameters. It provides an implicit representation of pore-scale structure by controlling the evolution of a pore size factor, thereby governing the width of hysteresis loops as well as the curvature and transition behavior between wetting and drying paths, without modifying the original functional forms of the selected models. Application of the framework to 10 SWRC models and 20 soil samples from the UNSODA database shows stable and consistent performance across a representative range of soil textures, with an average RMSE of 0.0133, while the majority of samples exhibit RMSE values below 0.025. Furthermore, analysis of higher-order scanning curves demonstrates that the framework can reproduce key features of path-dependent hysteresis, including main drying and wetting cycles and intermediate scanning behavior. Comparison with the widely used Kool-Parker hysteresis model further demonstrates that the proposed framework provides a more flexible representation of scanning behavior while requiring only one main drying or main wetting curve for primary curve characterization, with framework parameters calibrated from observed data.

title: Rapid temperature flips accelerate and amplify winter hypoxia and internal loading in a reservoir at the tropic of cancer
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Ya Zhu, Yiping Li, Yu Chen, Yaning Wang, Daobin Ji, Xingxing Zhao, Carlo Gualtieri, Martin Schmid
abstract: Although rapid temperature flips (RTFs) are recognized as an emerging form of climate variability, their effects on reservoir mixing and internal loading remain poorly constrained, especially in (sub)tropical reservoirs. Here, we integrated 12 months of high-frequency observations from Dawangtan Reservoir with three-year water-quality records and a mixed-layer mass-balance framework to examine how RTFs regulate winter hypoxia and the loading of reduced solutes (e.g., Fe2+, Mn2+, NH4 +). During the moderately warm winter of 2024, RTF frequency reached a five-decade high, driving repeated cycles of rapid mixing and short-lived restratification. These events caused sharp oscillations in Schmidt stability and thermocline depth, prevented sustained hypolimnetic reoxygenation, and produced synchronous increases in Mn and NH3-N as dissolved oxygen declined. Short recurrence intervals between RTFs resulted in the accumulation of oxygen deficits, ultimately causing whole-column anoxia. Rapid warm-cold flips entrained hypolimnetic water enriched with reduced solutes into the expanding mixed layer, whereas subsequent restratification allowed the depleted hypolimnetic solute pool to be replenished by sediment-derived solutes before the next mixing event. This transport–replenishment cycle, combined with shortened oxidation windows, concentrated internal loading into brief event periods. Four mixing events lasting only 25 days (6.8% of the year) accounted for 57.9% of annual Mn and 34.0% of annual NH3-N loads. Annual internal loads during 2023–2024 were over twice those in the previous two years. These findings show that intensified RTFs can convert gradual seasonal internal loading into abrupt winter water-quality shocks, highlighting the need for event-based monitoring and rapid reservoir–waterworks response under increasing climate variability.

title: Physics-guided symbolic regression of nonlocal transport memory from sparse observations in aquatic systems
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Xiangnan Yu, Yong Zhang, HongGuang Sun, Zhibo Chen, Yuntian Chen
abstract: Predicting non-Fickian transport in aquatic systems from sparse observations is challenging because historical effects and spatial heterogeneity often control present behavior. We introduce a physics-guided, sequential hybrid framework that couples nonlocal transport theory with deep-learning-assisted symbolic regression to infer transport memory directly from one-dimensional observations, such as breakthrough curves (BTCs) or spatial concentration snapshots. The physics module maps observations to a nonparametric memory representation derived from the statistics of microscopic particle dynamics, including temporal memory associated with mass-transfer-controlled transport and spatial (kinematic) memory represented by the streamtube velocity probability density function (PDF) for conductivity-driven spreading, thereby unifying temporal and spatial nonlocality within a single construct. Neural reconstruction, coupled with a stable numerical Laplace transform, produces denoised, high-resolution spectral representations, from which symbolic regression identifies compact, closed-form expressions for transport memory that are embedded back into the nonlocal model. Validation spans synthetic and experimental systems: semi-analytical fractional diffusion and a Cr(VI) column experiment (power-law kernels); a Red Cedar River tracer test (reach-specific, exponentially tempered kernels); random-walk particle tracking (Gamma-family velocity laws); groundwater tracer transport at the MADE field site (independently inferred inverse-Gamma velocity PDFs for MADE-1 and MADE-2 with out-of-sample predictive skill); and sediment transport in the North Loup River (a symmetric heavy-tailed velocity PDF capturing both backward and forward scaling). Across all cases, the inferred models reproduce observed transport behavior and accurately predict downstream profiles while remaining interpretable and parsimonious, without requiring quantitative prior characterization of aquatic system properties beyond geometry and boundary conditions. Compared to a purely data-driven sparse-regression approach on the same MADE-2 dataset, which yields only a near-integer-order advection equation ( α ≈ 1 ) with no dispersion, our physics-guided framework captures the anomalous spreading and predicts out-of-sample concentration snapshots, demonstrating enhanced robustness under sparse, noisy conditions. By bridging data-driven inference with nonlocal transport physics and expanding the concept of transport memory to encompass both temporal and spatial nonlocality, the proposed framework provides a practical and interpretable pathway for modeling anomalous transport under observational constraints common in laboratory and field hydrologic systems. This capability enables practical inference of transport memory and plume evolution in field systems where only sparse monitoring data are available, once the dominant transport mechanism has been qualitatively identified.

title: Spectral-enhanced cross-domain network: a novel daily runoff prediction model based on energy amplification and cross-domain multi-scale collaboration
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Ruohan Wang, Tao Yang
abstract: Accurate daily runoff forecasting is essential for water resources management and flood early warning, particularly in the context of intensifying climate change and anthropogenic pressures. However, existing deep learning models exhibit a spectral bias—a tendency to prioritize low-frequency trends over high-frequency signals—resulting in extreme- value smoothing that masks critical information about peak flows. Furthermore, single-perspective modeling paradigms struggle to disentangle the complex nonlinear dependencies of hydrological processes across the frequency, feature, and time domains. To address these challenges, we propose the Spectral-Enhanced Cross-domain Network (SEC), a novel daily runoff forecasting model that integrates a spectral energy modulator with cross-domain multi-scale collaboration. First, the Spectral Energy Modulator is proposed to enhance the capability of capturing flood rising points and low-flow fluctuations, mitigating the extreme-value smoothing problem inherent in traditional models by adaptively amplifying and recovering weak high-frequency abrupt signals in the frequency domain. Second, a Cross-Domain Multi-Scale Collaboration Mechanism is constructed, integrating Seasonal-Trend Decomposition, the Semi-Channel Interaction Block, and the Multi-scale Temporal Graph Neural Network. This architecture jointly models physical component separation, multivariate coupling, and local–global dependencies, providing a unified framework for non-stationary hydrological sequences. Experimental results conducted on natural catchments across six representative stations representing diverse hydro-climatic regions in the United States demonstrate that the SEC model comprehensively outperforms nine mainstream benchmark models, including PatchTST and TimesNet, in terms of NSE, KGE, MAE, and RMSE. SEC model achieved maximum NSE and KGE values of 0.977 and 0.986, respectively, reducing MAE by 0.6%–84.9% and RMSE by 2.8%–80.1%. This study demonstrates the utility of spectral energy modulation and cross-domain multi-Scale collaboration for modeling non-stationary hydrological sequences. The proposed framework provides an improved approach for analyzing extreme hydrological events and has potential for assisting in short-term extreme event forecasting.

title: High-spatiotemporal-resolution GRACE(-FO)-constrained terrestrial water storage reconstruction captures the hydrological footprints of successive typhoons in southern mainland China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Haotian Wu, Jiangjun Ran, Natthachet Tangdamrongsub, Yulong Zhong
abstract: The southern coastal region of mainland China faces persistent typhoon-related hydrological hazards, highlighting the need to monitor rapid variations in terrestrial water storage during extreme precipitation events. Satellite gravity missions provide observations of large-scale mass redistribution, but their coarse effective spatiotemporal resolution limits their ability to resolve short-lived, localized hydrological responses to typhoons. This study proposes a cascading framework that combines empirical-statistical reconstruction with machine-learning downscaling of reconstruction parameters to generate a climate-driven terrestrial water storage anomaly (TWSA) reconstruction at high spatiotemporal resolution. First, an improved empirical-statistical reconstruction model was calibrated against monthly GRACE(-FO) observations and used to reconstruct daily TWSA from precipitation and temperature data. Subsequently, the model parameters were spatially downscaled using XGBoost with climatic, topographic, soil, and vegetation predictors. The downscaled parameters were then reintroduced into the reconstruction model to generate daily TWSA at 0.1° spatial resolution. Cross-product comparisons with GRACE(-FO)-based products and estimates from land surface models showed overall consistency. Application of the framework in the Pearl River Basin during four successive typhoons in 2023 revealed distinct patterns in the reconstructed TWSA responses. During sustained post-landfall rainfall associated with Typhoon Haikui, reconstructed TWSA increased further to annual maxima across all four coastal sub-regions. The Pearl River Delta showed the largest increase, reaching 6.72 cm above the pre-typhoon baseline. These findings characterize cumulative and regionally heterogeneous reconstructed TWSA variations during successive typhoon events. The resulting dataset provides fine-scale information for characterizing extreme hydrological events and extends the utility of satellite gravity observations for studying rapid hydrological responses.

title: Integrated remote sensing retrieval of surface and root-zone soil moisture through physical mechanisms-guided machine learning
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Li Zhenghao, Yuan Qiangqiang, Yue Linwei, Yang Qianqian, Shen Huanfeng, Zhang Liangpei
abstract: Surface soil moisture (SSM) and root-zone soil moisture (RZSM), as key variables in the water cycle, play a crucial role in regulating water, energy, and carbon exchanges between the land surface and the atmosphere. Currently, satellite remote sensing retrieval technology is widely applied as an effective method for acquiring large-scale SSM data. However, the limited penetration capability of remote sensing signals into the soil presents significant challenges for the retrieval of RZSM. Physical and machine learning (ML) retrieval models require extensive labeled data to achieve high-accuracy retrieval, which poses difficulties in regions with limited in-situ data. To address these challenges, this study proposed an integrated retrieval framework for SSM and RZSM that combines physical mechanisms with ML models. This framework operates in two stages: in the first stage, a radiative transfer model based on brightness temperature data serves as the core, with the ML model employed to optimize the structure and parameters of the physical model, thereby enabling accurate retrieval of SSM. The SSM outputs subsequently serve as direct inputs for the subsequent stage. In the second stage, the ML retrieval model serves as the cornerstone, where the knowledge of soil moisture dynamics informs feature optimization to enable high-accuracy RZSM estimation. The retrieval framework demonstrated strong generalization and spatial extrapolation capabilities in jointly retrieving SSM and RZSM within the validation area in China. The development of this retrieval framework enables high-accuracy soil moisture retrieval in areas with limited monitoring sites, which lays the groundwork for generating large-scale soil moisture products, and provides robust data support for hydrological and climate-related research.

title: Integrating hydrogeomorphic changes into flood hazard assessment: approach for an eco-touristic mountainous river
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Marina R. Fagundes, Ronald E. Poeppl, Fernando M. Fan, Bruno H. Abatti, Gean P. Michel, Masato Kobiyama
abstract: Traditional flood risk assessments often overlook the hydrogeomorphic changes that occur during extreme events, despite their significant impact on subsequent flood behavior. This study investigates the influence of riverbed evolution on flood hazards in the Boi River catchment, located in a mountainous region in southern Brazil characterized by canyons, intense orographic precipitation, and ecotourism activities, through the application of the CAESAR-Lisflood Landscape Evolution Model. The Boi River has experienced recurrent flash floods that reshape its morphology. The model was calibrated using historical flood data, and its morphological response was locally evaluated at one downstream cross-section using pre- and post-event field surveys. Simulations were conducted for design storms with return periods of 2, 5, 25, and 100 years to analyze morphological changes, and the resulting Digital Elevation Models were then used as fixed terrain inputs in controlled RP002 simulations to isolate the hydraulic legacy of each individual antecedent event. Findings reveal that more extreme events cause significant bed aggradation and hydraulic spreading, altering flow depth, velocity, and hazard at selected exposed locations. Notably, the flood extent for a 2-year event increased by 16% when preceded by a 100-year event. A supplementary mobile-bed diagnostic for the RP100–RP002 case produced similar domain-wide inundation and HI-threshold exceedance results. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for sediment transport and morphological dynamics in flood hazard assessments. The CAESAR-Lisflood model provided a useful framework for exploring how flood-induced morphological changes may modify subsequent hazard patterns, although its morphological performance could only be evaluated locally.

title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of reference evapotranspiration in China (1981–2020): Insights into its teleconnection with sea surface temperature patterns
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Yudong Wang, Xin Lan, Mengyang Wu, Ahmed Elbeltagi, Juan Wang, Xinchun Cao
abstract: Reference evapotranspiration (ET0) governs agricultural irrigation water demand, yet its teleconnection with sea surface temperature (SST) patterns remains poorly understood under climate change. This study revealed the teleconnection between China’s ET0 and SST patterns based on the Penman-Monteith equation, multi-source data, machine learning models, and wavelet coherence analysis. Spatially, ET0 was highest in Northwest China (8.24 mm·d-1). Temporally, it increased significantly (0.0013 mm·d-1·yr−1, p < 0.05), peaking at 1.22 mm·d-1 in 2007. Multiple abrupt change points in ET0 coincided with strong Niño3.4, DMI and EMI events. SST patterns exert a clear phase-contrast influence on ET0: cold phases are predominantly associated with negative anomalies, whereas warm phases drive a widespread shift toward positive anomalies—especially during the WIOD phase, where the area with positive anomalies reaches 91.74%. Wavelet analysis reveals a significant multivariate synergistic enhancement effect between ET0 and SST patterns. The bivariate coupling of Niño3.4 + EMI exhibited the strongest explanatory power, with Average Wavelet Coherence (AWC) and Percentage Area of Significant Coherence (PASC) reaching 0.55 and 11.33%, respectively. When controlling for single-factor variables, the influence of DMI was more pronounced. Coupling of multiple SST patterns enhances the AWC with ET0, under the combined influence of all three SST patterns, the AWC reached 0.71. This study reveals that the synergistic effect of Niño3.4 and EMI on ET0 is stronger than that of any single SST pattern, providing new insights for agricultural water resource management under the impact of climate change.

title: Impacts of submarine groundwater discharge on inland and seaside basins of estuaries
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Qinbo Cheng, Yuyang Cai, Rongjiang Yao, Wenping Xie, Tianping Xu, Bradley A. Weymer, Xuan Yu
abstract: The interface between terrestrial aquifers and coastal water bodies, commonly described as a subterranean estuary, is increasingly recognized as an important pathway for freshwater and solute transport. Although the biogeochemical significance of submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) has been widely documented, the influence of groundwater–estuary exchange on estuarine hydrodynamics remains underrepresented in many surface-water modeling approaches. This study uses coupled surface water–groundwater modeling to quantify how a permeable-bed representation affects salinity, tidal storage, and transport across eight synthetic estuary types and three tidal amplitudes. Paired permeable- and impermeable-bed simulations used the same total freshwater input, although freshwater was delivered through the subsurface in the permeable cases and through the surface domain in the impermeable cases. The impermeable-bed simulations consistently produced higher estuarine salinity: in the reference tidal case, mean salinity ranged from 14.7 to 32.1 g/L, whereas the coupled permeable-bed representation reduced mean salinity by 0.1 to 8.8 g/L across estuary types. Permeable sediments also delayed the tidal response of inland-basin water storage, indicating that shallow subsurface exchange provides distributed transient storage that modifies basin filling and drainage. Particle-tracking diagnostics further showed that groundwater–estuary exchange alters transport pathways and residence behavior, with effects that depend strongly on estuary morphology and basin connectivity. These results show that treating the estuary bed as a no-flow boundary can bias predictions of salinity, residence behavior, and exchange pathways, with consequences for nutrient budgets, contaminant transport, and eutrophication management.

title: Glacial meltwater-driven suppression of riverine methane emissions in the high-altitude cryospheric regions
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Jiaxing Fu, Tanguang Gao, Meilin Chen, Xuexue Shang, Yulan Zhang, Liwei Zhang, Yongqin Liu, Shichang Kang
abstract: Headwater streams are widely recognized as hotspots of riverine methane (CH4) emissions; however, this understanding remains to be clarified in high-altitude cryospheric regions by the overriding influence of glacial meltwater. Based on chamber measurements from a four-year monitoring program (2020–2023) across 16 non-glacier-fed and 9 glacier-fed riverine sampling sites in the upper Heihe River of the northern Tibetan Plateau, we investigated the spatiotemporal dynamics of CH4 and evaluated the role of glacial meltwater in regulating riverine CH4 emissions. The results indicated that the downstream riverine sections of the upper Heihe River basin were weak atmospheric CH4 sources (0.39 ± 0.02 t CH4 yr−1). The riverine CH4 fluxes showed no significant correlation with river orders. This deviation is attributed primarily to the potent inhibitory effect of glacial meltwater. This suppression mechanism consists of a dual regulatory process: (1) thermal regulation, namely the relatively low temperatures of glacier meltwater can inhibit methanogenesis, and (2) biogeochemical dilution, namely the oligotrophic meltwater further reduced key methanogenic substrates (e.g., dissolved organic carbon). Consequently, the suppression can disturb seasonal variations in glacier-fed rivers and reduce overall watershed emissions by 13% ± 7% relative to a non-glacier-fed scenario. This study proposes a new conceptual framework for cryosphere-regulated hydro-biogeochemical coupling, highlighting the necessity of integrating these unique mechanisms into carbon cycle models for cryospheric regions.

title: Spatially distributed modeling of biofilm-induced hydrodynamic evolution in porous media
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Hongcheng Zhang, Chaomeng Dai, Jixiang Li, Jiajun Hu, Wang Kai Tong, Jia Jie Zou, Min-tian Gao, Zhi Li, Xihua Wang, Yalei Zhang, Kah Hon Leong, Swee Pin Yeap, Araceli Martín Candilejo
abstract: Biofilm growth in porous media significantly alters flow and transport properties in groundwater remediation, filtration and bioreactor operation, and membrane-related processes. However, most models treat biofilm zones as hydraulically uniform, neglecting internal heterogeneity and potentially compromising flow-field predictions. Here, we establish a spatially distributed framework for modeling the evolving hydrodynamics of biofilm growth in porous media by translating time-lapse biofilm images into distributed porosity and permeability fields, and evaluate it against the conventional uniform strategy. The results show that geometric heterogeneity promotes preferential colonization in narrow throats and the formation of larger pore-spanning clusters. Under the uniform strategy, multiple porosity–permeability combinations can reproduce the same bulk pressure drop and collapse onto a narrow compensation ridge (slope −11.15), revealing strong equifinality in hydraulic calibration and limited transferability of the calibrated parameters across growth stages. By contrast, the spatially distributed strategy reproduces the pressure drop evolution across growth stages. Although bulk pressure-drop calibration alone does not uniquely identify the absolute local values of n and k , the hydraulically admissible mappings yield effective hydraulic-property fields with broadly consistent spatial organization. Under the examined conditions, the resulting permeability distributions exhibit high-permeability tails that can be described by a Pareto-II distribution. Although both the uniform and spatially distributed strategies reproduce similar bulk pressure drops, the uniform treatment predicts more pronounced fast–slow segregation and velocity extremes. These findings establish a new framework for translating biofilm structure into hydraulically meaningful parameter fields, advancing predictive modeling of biofilm-driven hydrodynamics in porous media.

title: A routing-based approach to rank LID locations for runoff management at the watershed scale
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Yang Liu, Yuzhi Xiao, Anyang Tong, Shengle Cao, Guoqing Sang
abstract: Low Impact Development (LID) is widely used to mitigate urban flood runoff, yet selecting suitable locations at the watershed–scale remains challenging because hydrologic benefit depends on both local runoff-generation potential and upstream–downstream routing (the latter is often overlooked in previous research). We propose the Routing-Based LID Distribution Approach (RLDA), a routing-informed screening framework that ranks candidate locations by combining a Hydrologic Index (HI) and a Routing-Based Index (RBI) into a Comprehensive LID Benefit Index (CLBI). We discretize the watershed into Hydrologic Location Units, and represent LID options using permeable pavement and rain barrels. The framework was validated in the Xingjihe urban watershed in Jinan, China (294.78 ha), and further tested in the independent Green Acre Branch catchment. PySWMM is used to develop the catchment models to implement four deployment strategies, namely: CLBI-ranked, HI-ranked, RBI-ranked, uniform deployment, against a no-LID baseline deployment under four deployment budgets and five design storms (2-, 5-, 10-, 20-, and 50-year return periods). Across all return periods, the CLBI-ranked strategy generally produced the highest mean peak-flow reduction and total runoff reduction under the tested scenarios. However, the performance gap among strategies narrowed as storm intensity increased, indicating that routing-informed prioritization is most advantageous for frequent-to-moderate events while extreme storms increasingly overwhelm local controls. These findings provide an efficient, connectivity-aware ranking framework that bridges index-based screening and process-based validation for watershed–scale LID planning.

title: Duration-conditioned temporal profiles and synchronization networks reveal regional organization of midlatitude precipitation events
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Chun Zhou, Li Zhou, Luca Brocca, Xiaojun Guo, Ting Chen, Jiajia Yue, Keying Liu, Ming Li
abstract: Short-duration precipitation events are important drivers of flash floods and urban pluvial flooding, yet broad-scale comparisons of their within-event temporal structure and spatial coordination remain limited. We analyse quality-controlled hourly rain-gauge observations from the contiguous United States, selected European countries and Japan using a consistent event-based framework. Events are grouped by duration and characterized by peak-normalized within-event rainfall profiles; spatial coordination is evaluated with event-onset synchronization networks; and extreme events are analysed separately using regional 95th-percentile thresholds for peak intensity, event total and duration. Under the baseline 3 h minimum inter-event time, short- and medium-duration events account for 84.6% of the catalogue, whereas longer events are less frequent but more persistent. Short-duration events are widely represented, whereas longer-duration events show more localized areas of high station-level fraction. Network structure is strongly conditioned by gauge availability, and reference-density matching substantially reduces cross-domain differences in network degree. Over the region-specific effective analysis periods, Europe shows significant positive fitted slopes in extreme-event frequency and magnitude diagnostics, Japan shows no significant temporal changes, and the United States shows a significant decline only in extreme-event frequency. The extreme-event subset shows substantial regional overlap in principal component analysis space but distinct intensity–duration scaling: the Japanese station centroid is shifted toward higher scores on the magnitude-related second principal component, Japan shows the strongest increase in event total with duration, and the United States shows the steepest decline in peak intensity. These results provide a consistent event-based description of regional precipitation organization from hourly observations.

title: Projected intensification of compound river flooding and urban waterlogging in riverside cities of the Yangtze river basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Hong Du, Sidong Zeng, Yongyue Ji, Yating Hu, Zhuo Liu, Hayley J. Fowler, Jun Xia
abstract: Compound river flooding and urban waterlogging driven by fluvial and pluvial processes will increase flood risk in riverside cities. However, quantitative assessment of these compound flooding and waterlogging events (CFWE) remains challenging due to their complex dynamics and spatial heterogeneity. To address this, we propose a novel two-dimensional Composite Flooding and Waterlogging Index (CFWI) based on a nonstationary Copula-based framework incorporating antecedent hydrological conditions, which integrates both the severity and pattern of CFWE enabling identification of dominant contributions and facilitating consistent cross-regional comparison. The CFWI is applied to 48 riverside cities in the Yangtze River Basin, using hydrological simulations from the Distributed Time Variant Gain Model (DTVGM) driven by climate projections from ten CMIP6 global climate models under four Shared Socioeconomic Pathway scenarios (SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0, and SSP5–8.5). Results show that both the frequency and severity of CFWE increase under all future scenarios. The frequency of high flooding–high waterlogging (HFHW) events are most strongly in tributary subregions, while the severity of HFHW and high flooding–low waterlogging (HFLW) events intensifies primarily along the main reaches of the Yangtze River. Under natural conditions, CFWE hazards increase most markedly along the main river reach, with river flooding and urban waterlogging contributing approximately equally. However, when existing flood control and drainage capacities are considered, the largest increases in CFWE risk (approximately 0.3–0.6) occur in the upper reaches and tributary cities, while risk increases are smaller in the lower reaches (approximately 0.2). Across the basin, CFWE risk remains predominantly driven by urban waterlogging, highlighting persistent deficiencies in urban drainage systems, while river flooding becomes the primary driver of risk along the lower main reach. This study demonstrates that compound flooding in the Yangtze River Basin will become more frequent, more severe, and more spatially differentiated under climate change, and highlights the need to prioritise urban drainage capacity enhancement, particularly in tributary cities.

title: CO 2 migration and storage in layered saline aquifers: effects of vertical high-permeability channel width
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Wenyu Geng, Ke Chen, Jingru Zhang, Weiming Cheng, Yi Zhang, Lanlan Jiang, Yongchen Song
abstract: Deep saline aquifers in offshore regions are key storage sites for large-scale CO2 geological sequestration. However, multiple low-permeability cap rocks and localized high-permeability channels can strongly influence CO2 migration pathways and storage safety. This study addresses the limited understanding of the coupled effects of high-permeability channels on CO2 migration and multiple trapping mechanisms in multi-layer cap rock conditions. A two-dimensional numerical model based on geological characteristics in a South China Sea region was developed, and CO2 migration was systematically studied using CMG-GEM under two different vertical high-permeability channel widths (10 m and 50 m). The results show that channel width has a coupled influence on CO2 migration mechanisms: a 50 m wide channel accelerates pressure propagation and promotes horizontal CO2 migration (before entering the channel), while a 10 m wide channel exhibits a stronger flow focusing effect, enhancing vertical gas migration. The channel width significantly controls the accumulation and lateral diffusion of CO2 beneath different cap rocks, affecting the proportions of structural, dissolution, and residual storage. Salt precipitation occurs similarly across both scenarios but is more pronounced with wider channels, with the maximum reduction in porosity being approximately 0.076% for the 10 m channel and 0.11% for the 50 m channel, leading to a permeability decrease of about 0.23% and 0.33%, respectively. The impact on overall reservoir flow capacity is minimal. This study provides a quantitative assessment of the coupled effects of high-permeability channel width on CO2 sequestration, offering valuable insights for impact assessment and long-term safety analysis in offshore saline aquifer CO2 storage.

title: MEDAL: a mechanism-embedded dual-physics attention learning framework for snowmelt-driven runoff prediction in cold-region basins
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Miao Gu, Wen-chuan Wang, Kun-mei Luo, Can-can Shi, Dong-mei Xu
abstract: This study proposes a Mechanism-Embedded Dual-Physics Attention Learning (MEDAL) framework for daily runoff prediction in snowmelt-driven cold-region basins. As an architectural improvement to existing physics-guided hybrid modeling approaches, MEDAL employs the snowmelt-enhanced conceptual model SIMHYD-Snow as an upstream physical feature extractor to obtain static calibrated parameters and dynamic physical states, including snow water equivalent, soil moisture, and groundwater storage. These two types of information characterize the relatively stable physical boundary conditions of a basin and its dynamic hydrological memory, respectively. Building on this foundation, a dual-physics attention mechanism embeds both types of physical priors into meteorologically driven temporal representations, enabling them to jointly guide the selection of historical information across different hydrological stages. MEDAL achieved the best performance across all eight evaluation metrics in the five study basins. Ablation analyses in three representative basins further showed that, compared with the ablated models, MEDAL reduced mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean square error (RMSE) by an average of 31.3%–51.1% and 24.2%–35.2%, respectively, and its advantages across the five overall evaluation metrics were statistically significant (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Evaluations by year, season, and representative snowmelt event showed that MEDAL generally maintained stable advantages across different temporal subsets. Supplementary comparisons with two benchmark models adapted from recent physics-guided hybrid architectures further supported these findings. Under scenarios with 10% noise or missing data, the model achieved Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values above 0.9, indicating good robustness to data perturbations. Its one-step joint inference latency ranged from 1.35 to 2.17 ms, demonstrating the computational efficiency required for daily runoff prediction. The results indicate that, under the data and experimental conditions of this study, MEDAL can balance predictive accuracy, physical consistency, process interpretability, and computational efficiency, providing a physics-guided hybrid modeling approach for snowmelt-driven runoff prediction in cold regions.

title: Hillslope lag times for flood runoff are extremely short in high-relief meso-scale catchments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Takafumi Hajika, Yosuke Yamakawa, Taro Uchida
abstract: Understanding flood propagation in mountainous areas during heavy rainfall is crucial for disaster prevention. A previous study on flood propagation reported that the hillslope lag time is extremely short and almost negligible in meso-scale (1–10 km2) and medium-relief catchments. However, hydrological observations during heavy rainfall events in high-relief meso-scale catchments remain scarce. Therefore, this process has rarely been discussed. This study aimed to clarify flood propagation in high-relief meso-scale catchments with long and steep hillslopes. Seven mountain catchments (0.16–9.01 km2) underlain by accretionary sedimentary rock in Japan were investigated. Rainfall and water-level data over approximately 1.5 years were analyzed. The modal flow path lengths in the channel and hillslope at each site were calculated, and their relationships to the peak lag time (the time difference between rainfall and runoff peaks) were analyzed. Events showing a significant positive correlation between modal channel length and peak lag time accounted for only up to 15% of all events; in these events, hillslope lag time was estimated to be relatively uniform and extremely short (mean: −0.84 min; maximum: 160 min). This rapid hillslope response was confirmed even when the contributing area expanded. Conversely, some events exhibited a significant negative correlation. Although the lag time in larger catchments was similar to that observed in positively correlated events, a remarkably long peak lag time occurred in smaller catchments. This suggests that the initial rainfall loss and groundwater contribution may have been relatively greater in smaller catchments.

title: Toward transferable flash flood oriented high flow prediction in ungauged basins using a decoupled physics–DL framework
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Hyunjin Cho, Hyojun Bak, Gunhaeng Lee, Changhwan Kim, Hyejin Park, Dae-Hong Kim
abstract: Accurate flash flood prediction in ungauged basins remains a fundamental challenge. Process-based models often require extensive site-specific calibration, whereas end-to-end deep-learning (DL) models may lack physical consistency and can be difficult to transfer to ungauged settings. To address these limitations, we propose a decoupled physics–DL framework that separates the rainfall–runoff process into two components: physics-based surface runoff routing and a DL-based estimation of event-scale effective rainfall. Surface runoff was routed using a dynamic wave-based instantaneous unit hydrograph (DIUH) derived a priori from topographical and land-cover information, whereas rainfall losses were estimated by a multilayer perceptron (MLP) trained as a regionalization model using basin descriptors and rainfall event characteristics. The framework was evaluated using data from 62 basins in South Korea under a strict pseudo-ungauged design, in which 15 target basins were divided into three folds of five basins and each fold was withheld in turn for blind evaluation. In this evaluation, the framework achieved a median critical success index (CSI) of 0.50 under the strictest warning criteria, with the CSI increasing under more relaxed tolerance settings, and a median Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) of 0.75 for stage-hydrograph reproduction. The SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis further indicated that the MLP module produced statistically interpretable predictor–response patterns that were broadly consistent with the hydrological expectations. These results show that combining physics-based routing with regionalized DL hydrological loss estimations provides an effective and interpretable approach for flash flood oriented high flow prediction in pseudo-ungauged basins without local calibration in temperate monsoon-driven basins.

title: Unraveling meteorological contributions and lagged effects on multi-depth soil moisture prediction using Transformer-SHAP framework
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Jiankang Dong, Wenxue Xia, Huiqing Hao, Yi Lian, Furong Yu, Yonghong Hao, Tian-Chyi Jim Yeh
abstract: Soil moisture (SM) is a key state variable linking meteorological forcing with land surface hydrothermal processes. Accurate prediction of SM across soil depths and clarification of meteorological contributions and lagged effects are important. Here, meteorological contributions refer to the SHAP quantified contributions of individual predictors to SM predictions, whereas lagged effects refer to the historical period over which antecedent meteorological information remains useful for predicting current SM. We developed separate Transformer models for the 5, 20, 45, and 80 cm soil layers and identified the optimal historical input window for each depth. The models achieved NSE values of 0.82, 0.78, 0.70, and 0.90, respectively. The optimal windows increased from 20 days at 5 cm to 21, 29, and 40 days at 20, 45, and 80 cm, indicating longer dependence on antecedent meteorological information with increasing depth.
